title: Fictional: the Halvek Pass combined targeting cell
question: Did the Republic of Calvaro breach its obligations under the Convention on Cluster Munitions when its co-director of the combined targeting cell signed the tasking order for the strike near Halvek Pass?
facts: An international armed conflict has existed since March 2025 between the Republic of Calvaro and the Federation of Drennick. The Kingdom of Sorvenia, which is not a party to the Convention on Cluster Munitions, entered the conflict as Calvaro's ally in June 2025. Calvaro has been a party to the Convention on Cluster Munitions since 2012; Drennick is not a party. Calvaro formally notified Sorvenia of its obligations under the Convention and urged it not to use cluster munitions. The two allies set up a Combined Air Targeting Cell co-directed by a Calvaran colonel and a Sorvenian colonel. Under the cell's written procedures, every tasking order, including the munition to be used, takes effect only when signed by both co-directors, and neither can change the munition alone. Only Sorvenian aircraft fly the cell's missions. On 3 October 2025 the Sorvenian co-director proposed a strike on a Drennick armoured column near Halvek Pass using air-delivered cluster munitions. The Calvaran co-director raised no objection to the munition and signed the tasking order, which specified cluster munitions. Sorvenian aircraft carried out the strike that day using cluster munitions.
holding: Authored ground truth for a fictional case; no tribunal has ruled on it. Indeterminate. Article 21(3) permits a State Party and its personnel to engage in military cooperation and operations with states not party that might engage in prohibited activities, but Article 21(4) does not authorise a State Party to itself use cluster munitions or to expressly request their use where the choice of munitions is within its exclusive control. Here the choice was jointly controlled, not within Calvaro's exclusive control, and Calvaro did not itself deliver the munitions, so Article 21(4)(c) and (d) are not clearly engaged. Whether co-signing an order that specifies cluster munitions is protected cooperation under Article 21(3), or is assistance or encouragement prohibited by Article 1(1)(c), depends on how the two provisions interact, which the text of the Convention does not resolve and on which states parties have taken differing positions.
key_reasoning: Article 21(3) permits military cooperation and operations with non-party states that might engage in prohibited activities, notwithstanding Article 1.

Article 21(4)(d) forbids expressly requesting the use of cluster munitions only where the choice of munitions is within the State Party's exclusive control; here the choice required both co-directors' signatures, so control was shared.
Article 21(4)(c) forbids the State Party itself using cluster munitions; Calvaro did not deliver them, but its co-director's signature was a necessary condition of the order taking effect.

Whether that signature is permitted cooperation or prohibited assistance or encouragement under Article 1(1)(c) turns on the unsettled relationship between Articles 1 and 21, which the treaty text does not determine.
